---
title: "Naive gene screen"
---

## Building $\mathcal{G}_{0}$ {#sec-fs-naive}

This chapter builds a working universe $\mathcal{G}_{0}$ on which a GGM
can be estimated. Genes are scored from one labelled single-cell
reference, used as a **signature**, not from a multi-sample atlas.
Global ranks (highly variable genes) and a short knowledge-driven marker
list both remove genes from the whole transcriptome. The all-versus-all
refinement that uses $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}$ comes **after** GRN
inference (@sec-fs-advanced).

Notation: gene $g=1,\ldots,G$; cell type $j=1,\ldots,J$; cell
$c=1,\ldots,C$. A cell labelled as type $j$ is written $c_{j}$. Bulk
samples stay indexed by $i$, as in the article. The DeCovarT convolution
is linear in $\boldsymbol{p}$ only on an additive scale
(@nte-linear-scale).

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-fs-naive
%%| fig-cap: "Naive screen on one labelled single-cell reference: Pearson-residual ranking and a short knowledge-driven marker list. No DESeq2 p-values."
%%{init: {"theme": "sandstone", "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": true}}}%%
flowchart TD
  A["UMI y_cg, labels j"] --> B["Technical NB null, library size only"]
  B --> C["Pearson residuals r_cg"]
  C --> D["Rank by between versus within type"]
  E["Knowledge markers"] --> F["Gene universe G_0"]
  D --> F
  F --> G["GGM chapter"]
```

::: {#nte-linear-scale .callout-important}
## :warning: Keep the mixture on a linear scale

The convolution
$\boldsymbol{y}\mid(\boldsymbol{\zeta},\boldsymbol{p})\sim\mathcal{N}_{G}(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p},\sum_{j}p_{j}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j})$
is linear in $\boldsymbol{p}$ only if $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ and $\boldsymbol{y}$ live
on the **same additive scale** (counts, CPM, or TPM). Logarithms,
`SCTransform` Pearson residuals, and nonparanormal scores break that
map [@sturmComprehensiveEvaluationTranscriptomebased2019;
@jinBenchmarkRNAseqDeconvolution2021;
@hoffmannRobustComputationalReconstitution2006]. Use residualisation
only to **rank** genes; export DeCovarT moments on the linear scale.
Non-affine maps (logarithms, Pearson residuals, nonparanormal scores)
change the estimand by Jensen's inequality.
:::

## Highly variable genes as a signal-to-noise rank {#sec-fs-hvg}

Single-cell UMI tables mix depth noise with biological heterogeneity.
Regularised negative-binomial regression in `sctransform`
[@R-sctransform] / `Seurat::SCTransform` separates the two via Pearson
residuals [@hafemeisterNormalizationVarianceStabilization2019]. We use
that transform **only to rank genes**, not to normalise the table that
enters glasso or PLN, and not as a factorial arm of the GRN design
(@sec-grn-observation).

On this single-cell reference the only technical covariate we actually
have is **library size**. There is a single scRNA-seq resource, so
batch, donor and unmeasured technical branches cannot be identified
[@hafemeisterNormalizationVarianceStabilization2019]. The technical
null is therefore

$$
\log\mu_{cg}
=
\beta_{0g}
+
\operatorname{offset}(\log L_{c}),
\qquad
y_{cg}\sim\mathrm{NB}(\mu_{cg},\theta_{g}),
$$ {#eq-fs-nb-null}

with $L_{c}$ the library size of cell $c$. **Do not** put cell type
$j$ in this null: that would remove the between-type signal the panel
is meant to keep.

Pearson residuals are

$$
r_{cg}
=
\frac{y_{cg}-\hat{\mu}_{cg}}
{\sqrt{\hat{\mu}_{cg}+\hat{\mu}_{cg}^{2}/\hat{\theta}_{g}}}.
$$ {#eq-fs-pearson}

@fig-sct-pearson recalls the NB mean–variance relation and the residual
scale used by `SCTransform`.

![`SCTransform` negative-binomial mean–variance relation and Pearson
residuals (Seurat v5).](images/scTransform_computation-1.png){#fig-sct-pearson}

### Total, biological, and technical pieces

For gene $g$ write $V_{\mathrm{total},g}=\mathrm{Var}_{c}(r_{cg})$ for
residual variation after the depth null. That leftover is **not** pure
biology: it still contains model misspecification. What we can split
with the labels $j$ is biological variation **between** versus
**within** cell types,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{between},g}
&=
\sum_{j=1}^{J}
C_{j}
\bigl(\bar{r}_{gj}-\bar{r}_{g}\bigr)^{2},
\qquad
\bar{r}_{gj}
=
C_{j}^{-1}\sum_{c_{j}}r_{c_{j}g},\\
\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{within},g}
&=
\sum_{j=1}^{J}
\sum_{c_{j}}
\bigl(r_{c_{j}g}-\bar{r}_{gj}\bigr)^{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-fs-ss}

$C_{j}$ is the number of cells labelled $j$. Because the residuals are
globally approximately centred, $\bar{r}_{g}\approx 0$ and
$\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{between},g}\approx\sum_{j}C_{j}\bar{r}_{gj}^{2}$.
A lineage marker (high between-type, low within-type) is the gene we
want. A stress-response gene (low between-type, high within-type) is
not, even if its **total** residual variance is large.
@fig-pearson-sources sketches that split.

![Technical variation absorbed by a library-size negative-binomial null,
and biological residual variation split into between-type and
within-type pieces.](images/pearson_residual_variance_sources.png){#fig-pearson-sources}

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| label: fig-fs-varsplit
%%| fig-cap: "Residual variance after a library-size NB null. Technical variation is whatever the null absorbed; leftover variation is split into between-type and within-type biological pieces. Rank genes by a high between / low within ratio, not by total residual variance alone."
%%{init: {"theme": "sandstone", "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": true}}}%%
flowchart TD
  Y["y_cg"] --> N["NB technical null: offset log L_c only"]
  N --> R["Pearson r_cg"]
  R --> T["Total residual variance"]
  T --> B["Between type"]
  T --> W["Within type"]
  B --> S["Keep high between, low within"]
  W --> S
```

There is **no** calibrated differential-expression $p$-value here: one
technical replicate cannot support `DESeq2` (@nte-pseudoreplication).
The between-type sum of squares is a **ranking score**.

Use `Seurat::SCTransform()` with Pearson residuals
(`vst.flavor = "v2"`). That **is** the residual transformation used to
rank genes (@nte-sct-v1-v2).

After `SCTransform`, pull the residual matrix and compute
@eq-fs-ss by the labelled type $j$. Keep on the order of $2{,}000$
genes in $\mathcal{G}_{0}$ before any GGM
[@friedmanSparseInverseCovariance2008].

```{r}
#| label: sct-snr-rank
#| eval: false
# Sketch: Pearson residuals for ranking only; export counts to the GGM.
sct <- Seurat::SCTransform(
  seu,
  method = "glmGamPoi",
  residual.feature = NULL,
  return.only.var.genes = FALSE,
  vst.flavor = "v2"
)
R <- Seurat::GetAssayData(sct, assay = "SCT", layer = "scale.data")
# rows gene g, columns cell c; align with cell-type factor j
j <- sct$celltype
ss_between <- apply(R, 1, function(r) {
  means <- tapply(r, j, mean)
  n_j <- tapply(r, j, length)
  sum(n_j * means^2)
})
ss_within <- apply(R, 1, function(r) {
  sum(tapply(r, j, function(z) sum((z - mean(z))^2)))
})
snr <- ss_between / pmax(ss_within, .Machine$double.eps)
```

::: {#nte-sct-v1-v2 .callout-note}
## :information_source: `vst.flavor = "v2"` still returns Pearson residuals

Both flavours of `SCTransform` assume
$Y_{cg}\sim\mathrm{NB}(\mu_{cg},\theta_{g})$ and store Pearson residuals.
What changes is the fit that produces $\hat\mu_{cg}$ and $\hat\theta_{g}$
(@fig-sct-v1-v2).

In v1 the depth slope is a gene-wise coefficient,

$$
\log\mu_{cg}=\beta_{0g}+\beta_{1g}\log_{10}(n_{c}).
$$

In v2 that slope is fixed at $\ln 10$, so library size is an offset
[@choudharyComparisonEvaluationStatistical2022;
@lauseAnalyticPearsonResiduals2021]:

$$
\log\mu_{cg}=\beta_{0g}+\log n_{c},
\qquad
\mu_{cg}=e^{\beta_{0g}}\,n_{c}.
$$

Doubling the UMI depth then doubles every gene's expected count. v2
also regularises dispersions with the `glmGamPoi` offset route, treats
genes with no evidence of overdispersion as Poisson
($\theta_{g}=\infty$), and floors the Pearson denominator at a minimum
variance (`min_variance = "umi_median"`) before the separate residual
clip. The ranking above uses those v2 residuals; it does not use
Seurat's variable-feature shortlist.

![Shared negative-binomial model, and the v1 gene-wise depth slope
versus the v2 offset.](images/sctransform_v1_versus_v2.png){#fig-sct-v1-v2}
:::

### Design used for the naive screen {#sec-fs-sct-design}

::: {#nte-fs-prefilter .callout-warning}
## :warning: What is removed before the v2 fit

The regression is not run on the full transcriptome. Three filters
change which residuals enter the rank.

1. **Gene allow-list.** Of 27,027 genes in the RNA assay, the author
   SCT `counts` layer keeps 2,944 symbols. The remaining genes are
   treated as having failed the authors' bare QC and never enter the
   negative-binomial fit.
2. **Residual clip.** `SCTransform` winsorises Pearson residuals at
   $\pm\sqrt{n/30}$ before they are used downstream. On the fitted
   slots that bound is about $\pm 19.1$ at 48 h ($n = 10{,}891$),
   $\pm 12.4$ at 72 h ($n = 4{,}619$) and $\pm 12.8$ at 96 h
   ($n = 4{,}935$). The clip limits the leverage of a few cells with
   extreme counts, so one barcode cannot dominate a sum of squares.
   The leading genes are not a short list of single-cell spikes: at
   48 h the top ratios are modest and land on naïve-pluripotency
   markers, and at 96 h the top gene is the endoderm marker *Sox17*.
   The bound is wide relative to a unit-variance residual, so it
   changes only the far tail.
3. **Cell-type filter.** Culture-stress labels (Cd63+ ectoderm-like
   artefact, Zscan4+ artefact) are dropped before the fit. A type with
   fewer than 20 cells in a slot is kept in the fit and then left out
   of the sums of squares. Exiting naïve pluripotency at 72 h has 8
   cells and is not scored.
:::

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-fs-prefilter
%%| fig-cap: "Pre-filter, v2 fit, and the two global rankings."
%%{init: {"theme": "sandstone"}}%%
flowchart TD
  A["27,027 RNA genes"] --> B["2,944 symbols in the SCT counts layer"]
  B --> C["Drop culture-stress labels"]
  C --> D["SCTransform v2 per time slot"]
  D --> E["Clip Pearson residuals at ±sqrt of n over 30"]
  E --> F["Leave out types with fewer than 20 cells"]
  F --> G["Equal-cell sums of squares"]
  F --> H["Equal-type mean squares, weight 1/J"]
  G --> I["Top 500 genes"]
  H --> I
```

`sctransform::vst()` with `vst.flavor = "v2"` is an intercept plus a
library-size offset. There is no richer design matrix on this object
that we can identify.

The fitted mean, for each gene $g$ and cell $c$, is

$$
\log\mu_{cg}
=
\beta_{0g}
+
\operatorname{offset}(\log L_{c}),
\qquad
\mu_{cg}
=
e^{\beta_{0g}} L_{c},
$$ {#eq-fs-v2-offset}

with $L_{c}$ the full RNA library size (column sum of the unfiltered
count matrix), not the sum over the gene allow-list. In the
implementation the offset is $\log L_{c}$ and the stored slope on
$\log_{10} L_{c}$ is the constant $\ln 10$. When `glmGamPoi` is
installed the fitter is `glmGamPoi_offset`; otherwise v2 falls back to
the same offset model (`nb_offset`). `vars.to.regress` is empty.

What we deliberately leave out:

- **Cell type** is not a covariate. Putting $j$ in the null would
  remove the between-type residual the rank is meant to keep
  (@eq-fs-ss).
- **Cell line** (B-S versus SBR) is not a covariate. It is confounded
  with time except at 48 h (@sec-geo-design), and the chapter treats
  the two lines as equivalent trajectories.
- **Time** is not a column inside one regression. The negative-binomial
  fit is repeated **independently at 48 h, 72 h and 96 h**, which are
  the slots shared with the bulk HTSeq table. Cells of every retained
  type at that slot are fitted together. A single fit across times
  would mix stage differences into the residuals; a time coefficient
  would partial those differences out of a contrast we want to make
  inside each slot, where the GRN is learned.


Three lists are built after the residual split, then each list is united with the
signalling markers of the cell types actually scored in that time slot
(`data/dictionaries/mouse_gastruloid_signaling_markers.csv`, symbols
mapped offline with `org.Mm.eg.db`, not biomaRt):

1. **Global, equal cell weight.** Top `n_genes_global` genes by
   $\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{between}}/\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{within}}$
   (default 500). Every barcode contributes equally, so the largest
   type dominates the sums of squares. The cap sits below the
   few-thousand ceiling suggested before a GGM and is an argument of
   the script.
2. **Global, equal type weight.** The same cap of 500, with each of
   the $J$ scored types given weight $1/J$. Let $\bar r_{gj}$ be the
   mean residual of gene $g$ in type $j$ and $v_{gj}$ the within-type
   variance. The equal-type mean and the two mean squares are
   $$
   \bar r_{g}^{\mathrm{eq}}
   =
   J^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{J}\bar r_{gj},
   \quad
   \mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm{between},g}
   =
   J^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{J}
   (\bar r_{gj}-\bar r_{g}^{\mathrm{eq}})^{2},
   \quad
   \mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm{within},g}
   =
   J^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{J} v_{gj}.
   $$ {#eq-fs-equal-type}
   Genes are ranked by
   $\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm{between}}/\mathrm{MS}_{\mathrm{within}}$.
3. **Per cell type.** One-versus-rest ANOVA, top
   `n_genes_celltype` genes by the equal-cell ratio (default 50).
   $\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{between}}>\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{within}}$
   is recorded and drawn, and is not a hard gate. Pearson residuals
   are scaled to unit variance, so that inequality is an $R^{2}>1/2$
   cut and almost no gene meets it when one type dominates the slot.

Culture-stress labels in
`data/dictionaries/suppinger_celltype_crosswalk.csv` are dropped before
the fit. Types with fewer than `min_cells` cells (default 20) in a slot
stay out of the sum of squares. The entry points are
`scripts/01_01_prepare_and_filter_genes_sctransform.R` and
`scripts/01_02_plot_naively_selected_genes.R`.
`scripts/01_03_sensitivity_48h_cell_line.R` refits the same v2 model
inside B-S and inside SBR at 48 h, the only slot that contains both
lines, and compares the equal-cell top 500 and the per-type top 50.
Those two global lists share 308 of 500 genes (Jaccard 0.45). Epiblast
and exiting naïve pluripotency share 29 and 30 of their top 50.
Naïve pluripotency is scored only in SBR: B-S has fewer than 20 cells
of that type.

::: {#nte-hvg-not-gaussian .callout-note}
## :information_source: HVGs are not a GGM input

Pearson residuals are closer to homoscedastic than raw UMI counts,
which is why they are popular before PCA. They are still a **nonlinear
residualisation**. Feeding them indiscriminately into `SILGGM` silently
changes the estimand of $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}$ away from the latent
Gaussian that DeCovarT wants at the **population** level. If a Gaussian
GGM is used, prefer a copula / nonparanormal map on the same gene set
(@sec-silggm), or better a Poisson-lognormal latent Gaussian
(@sec-pln).
:::

## Marker genes {#sec-fs-markers}

Shannon entropy and Gini of relative means are compaction scores for
long one-versus-rest lists. Definitions live in the DeCovarT vignette
[supp-S6-feature-selection.qmd](https://github.com/bastienchassagnol/DeCovarT/blob/main/vignettes/supp-S6-feature-selection.qmd#L62-L254).

On this reference the marker list is **knowledge-driven** and already
short. It is stored as

`data/dictionaries/mouse_gastruloid_signaling_markers.csv`

with three columns: `cell_type_excel` (lineage name on the signalling
map), `cell_type_suppinger` (the matching Suppinger label, or `NA` when
that lineage is absent), and `gene_marker`. Because the list is a
curated biological seed rather than a concatenated differential-expression
shortlist, it does not by itself inflate collinearity of
$\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{G}}$. Seeds may later be grown by Markov
boundaries (@sec-separation).

Fifteen of the 19 mouse symbols fall in the 2,944-gene SCT allow-list.
Under a uniform draw of 19 genes from the 27,027 RNA symbols, the
expected overlap is about 2.1. The upper tail probability is
$P(X \ge 15) = 8.8 \times 10^{-12}$
(hypergeometric; population 27,027, 2,944 marked as the allow-list,
draw of 19). The four markers absent from the allow-list are
*Myod1*, *Pax6*, *Sox1* and *Tfap2a*. They are drawn on
`venn_markers_vs_counts.pdf`.

## What we would actually run

1.  `SCTransform` Pearson residuals under @eq-fs-v2-offset, separately
    at 48 h, 72 h and 96 h (@sec-fs-sct-design). Rank by between/within
    @eq-fs-ss with equal cell weight, and by the equal-type mean
    squares @eq-fs-equal-type. Global cap 500 genes on each ranking;
    per type, top 50 by the equal-cell ratio.
2.  Union with
    `data/dictionaries/mouse_gastruloid_signaling_markers.csv`
    for cell types scored in that time slot (drop rows with
    `cell_type_suppinger` missing unless a later reference needs them).
3.  Keep $|\mathcal{G}_{0}|$ on the order of a few thousand genes before
    a GGM. The naive screen above is a tighter, tunable subset.
4.  **No** `DESeq2` $p$-values on technical sc pseudo-bulks; see
    @sec-fs-deg for `MAST` when an omnibus cell-type test is needed.
    For a calibrated gene threshold instead of a fixed rank cap, see
    @sec-fs-permutation.

## Permutation calibration of between-type signal {#sec-fs-permutation}

The naive screen ranks genes by the between/within split in
@eq-fs-ss. An alternative is to **calibrate** that signal against a
null in which cell type and expression are unrelated, and to set the
shortlist from empirical $p$-values or a multiplicity-adjusted
threshold rather than from a fixed top-$G$ cut.

::: {#nte-f-anova .callout-note}
## :information_source: The usual $F$ statistic and its assumptions

For gene $g$, with $J$ cell types, $N$ cells and type counts $C_j$,
the one-way ANOVA $F$-ratio compares **between-type** and
**within-type** mean squares built from @eq-fs-ss:

$$
F_g
=
\frac{\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{between},g}/(J-1)}
     {\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{within},g}/(N-J)}.
$$ {#eq-fs-fanova}

Large $F_g$ means type means differ relative to scatter inside types.
Under a **classical** linear model the null distribution of $F_g$ is
$F_{J-1,\,N-J}$ when, for that gene,

- residuals are **homoscedastic** across types and cells;
- observations are **independent** (or the design is balanced enough
  that the usual ANOVA table still targets the intended contrast);
- within-type residuals are **Gaussian** (or $N$ is large enough that
  the ratio is still usable).

The **degrees-of-freedom** correction in @eq-fs-fanova matters: a raw
ratio $\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{between}}/\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{within}}$
without dividing by $J-1$ and $N-J$ is not the same estimand and should
not be read off the $F$ table. The naive bar plots report the
**share** $\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{between}}/(\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{between}}+\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{within}})$ for
interpretation; @eq-fs-fanova is the inferential counterpart.
:::

On single-cell Pearson residuals those assumptions are **unlikely** to
hold gene by gene: genes are **correlated**, variances differ with
mean and detection rate, and tails are heavy after SCTransform
clipping. Treating $F_g$ as $F_{J-1,\,N-J}$ therefore mis-calibrates
the tail. A **permutation** scheme keeps the same $F_g$ (or the same
between/within ratio used in the screen) but estimates its null from
replicated label randomisations, yielding gene-wise
$p_g=(1+\sum_b I(F_g^{(b)}\ge F_g^{\mathrm{obs}}))/(B+1)$ and,
optionally, Benjamini–Hochberg FDR or a single **max-$F$** cutoff from
the permutation maxima $M_b=\max_g F_g^{(b)}$.

**Cell-type label shuffling, not gene shuffling.** Apply one
permutation of cell indices to **all genes** at once. Each gene keeps
its marginal residual distribution, sparsity and gene–gene dependence;
only the link $R_g \perp C$ is broken. That is the null
$H_{0g}:$ cell type carries no extra information about gene $g$
beyond chance assignment. **Gene-label** permutations do not generate
that null: renaming columns leaves the empirical $F$ distribution
unchanged; independent shuffles within cells destroy marginal structure
and treat genes as exchangeable, which SCTransform residuals are not.

**Nuisance structure.** With only cell type in the model, permute labels
(optionally **within donor** or batch strata so group sizes and
exchangeability match the design). With fixed covariates
(donor, batch, condition, …), naive global label swaps can create
impossible factor combinations. Then use **Freedman–Lane** residual
permutation [@freedmanNonstochasticInterpretation1983]: fit the
**reduced** model without cell type, obtain residuals $e_g$, and form
$R_g^{*}=\hat R_{0g}+P e_g$ with the **same** row permutation $P$ for
every gene; refit the full model and recompute $F_g$. The response is
the matrix of Pearson residuals (or another downstream quantity); the
“residuals” being permuted are from the **biological** linear predictor
that holds nuisance terms fixed, not a blind shuffle of SCTransform
Pearson residuals across cells. The `glmperm` package implements the
same shuffle-$R$ idea for GLMs via permutation of regressor residuals
[@werftGlmpermPermutation2010]. In regression we typically test the
**conditional mean** given covariates, not the raw expression margin.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-fs-permutation-choice
%%| fig-cap: "Choosing a classical F test versus label or Freedman–Lane permutation for the between-type signal."
%%{init: {"theme": "sandstone", "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": true}}}%%
flowchart TD
  A["Matrix R: cells by genes; type labels and covariates"] --> B{"Classical one-way ANOVA assumptions acceptable?"}
  B -->|Yes| C["F_g with SS and df from eq-fs-fanova"]
  C --> D["Compare to F_{J-1, N-J} or GLM F test"]
  B -->|No| E{"Nuisance covariates absent?"}
  E -->|Yes| F["Permute cell-type labels; same permutation for all genes"]
  E -->|No| G["Freedman–Lane: fit reduced model without cell type"]
  G --> H["Permute rows of biological residuals; refit full model"]
  F --> I["Empirical p_g; BH FDR or max-F threshold"]
  H --> I
  D --> J["Fixed alpha or FDR on analytic p-values"]
```

This chapter does **not** run that permutation pipeline on GSE229513;
it records the design choice. When implemented, use the **identical**
statistic in every replicate and document whether labels are permuted
globally or within strata.

::: {#nte-permutation-circularity .callout-warning}
## :warning: Double dipping and post-clustering inference

Permutation $p$-values are only meaningful if the **labels tested** are
fixed **before** the statistic is defined on the same matrix. If cell
types were **estimated** by clustering (or refined post hoc) on the same
expression that enters $F_g$, the test reuses information that built
the groups: apparent between-type separation is inflated and
$p$-values are anti-conservative. The same circularity arises when
genes are chosen because they **define** clusters and are then
reported as “markers” of those clusters.

Post-clustering and post-selection inference formalise this bias:
hypotheses must be corrected for the **selection event** (selective
type I error), not treated as if labels were exogenous
[@gonzalezDelgadoPostclusteringInference2025]. Practical mitigations
include held-out cells or donors, pre-specified author annotations,
prospective marker lists (as in @sec-fs-markers), or selective
inference machinery—not rerunning a label permutation on labels that the
data helped create.
:::

## Differential expression — only with biological replication {#sec-fs-deg}

`DESeq2`, `edgeR` and `limma`–voom remain the workhorses of
one-versus-rest ranking [@loveModeratedEstimationFold2014]. That logic
**does not transfer** to GSE229513 as a DE experiment.

::: {#nte-pseudoreplication .callout-warning}
## :warning: Technical pseudo-bulks are not biological replicates

Cells from a common experimental unit are not independent biological
replicates. Splitting or bootstrapping cells characterises
**technical / sampling** variability; it does not manufacture
between-organoid uncertainty. Treating cells, or random partitions of
cells, as `DESeq2` replicates inflates apparent degrees of freedom and
produces false discoveries [@squairConfrontingFalseDiscoveries2021;
@crowellMuscatDetectsSubpopulationspecific2020].

Use `DESeq2` in this book only if **independent biological replicates**
exist at the level of the contrast (for example, organoids or animals).
For omnibus **cell-type** contrasts on single cells without a valid
pseudo-bulk design, prefer the `MAST` hurdle workflow (@nte-mast-omnibus)
over `DESeq2`. For GSE229513, skip calibrated DE $p$-values. Rank genes
by @eq-fs-ss or by the knowledge table, not by a nested-model $F$
treated as a $p$-value.

Bulk HTSeq tables (GSE229386) **do** have three biological replicates
per time and Wnt schedule (@sec-geo-design). Those replicates support
**bulk** DE of treatments, not cell-type GRNs from the scRNA-seq
object.
:::

::: {#nte-mast-omnibus .callout-note}
## :information_source: Omnibus cell-type testing with `MAST`

When the goal is **which genes differ among annotated cell types on
single cells**, but there are no independent biological replicates to
feed a pseudo-bulk `DESeq2` design, the cell-level hurdle model in
`MAST` [@finakMASTFlexibleStatistical2015] is the usual alternative.
It keeps one row per cell, models dropout and expression on the
log-normalised scale, and adjusts for cellular detection rate
(`cngeneson`, the scaled number of genes detected per cell).

Fit a **full** model with `MAST::zlm()`: cell type and any nuisance
factors (condition, sex, batch, …) as **fixed** effects, plus
`(1 | sample_id)` when true biological replicates exist. Compare to a
**reduced** model that drops only the whole `cell_type` factor, using
`MAST::lrTest(fit, "cell_type")`. That likelihood-ratio test is the
omnibus analogue of a multi-level ANOVA: it does **not** enumerate
pairwise one-versus-rest contrasts.

Each gene yields three $p$-values: **discrete** (`disc`), whether
detection probability differs among types; **continuous** (`cont`),
whether positive expression magnitude differs among types; and
**hurdle** (`hurdle`), which combines the two components. For feature
shortlists, require both `disc` and `cont` to be small (or use the
combined hurdle with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR), then keep genes that are
detected in a minimal subset of types, not only significant on
dropout-driven signal. The omnibus test has **no single log-fold-change
direction**; after global LRT and FDR, inspect type means or run
selected post-hoc contrasts only for genes that pass the hurdle.

With a **single** organoid or donor, the estimand is variation **within
that specimen**, not a population claim across individuals. That
matches GSE229513 for exploratory ranking, but it does not replace the
Pearson-residual screen in this chapter when batch and time are
confounded.
:::

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-fs-mast-omnibus
%%| fig-cap: "MAST omnibus workflow for cell-type differential expression when pseudo-bulk DESeq2 is inappropriate."
%%{init: {"theme": "sandstone", "flowchart": {"htmlLabels": true}}}%%
flowchart TD
  A["Log-normalised RNA matrix and cell metadata"] --> B["SingleCellAssay; standardise cngeneson"]
  B --> C["MAST::zlm full model"]
  C --> D["cell_type plus fixed covariates"]
  C --> E["(1 | sample_id) when biological replicates exist"]
  D --> F["MAST::lrTest fit, cell_type"]
  E --> F
  F --> G["Reduced model drops cell_type only"]
  G --> H["Per gene: disc, cont, hurdle LRT"]
  H --> I["BH FDR on hurdle; check disc and cont"]
  I --> J["Keep genes detected across a minimal type subset"]
  J --> K["Post-hoc means or contrasts on significant genes only"]
```

### Differential networks {#sec-fs-perspective}

These methods are **not** in the naive screen. They need graphs, so
they nominate extras for $\mathcal{G}_{0}$ **after** a first GGM pass.
Full algebraic detail of `INDEED` and D-trace lives in DeCovarT
`vignettes/supp-S6-feature-selection.qmd`. Separation language
(directed versus undirected) is in @sec-separation.

DeCovarT benefits from **rewiring** between populations. A gene that
changes neighbourhood in $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}$ is a better candidate
than a gene that is merely highly variable.

**Fit every $\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}$, then compare supports.** Independent
glasso / `SILGGM` fits (@sec-silggm) yield per-type edges; the symmetric
difference of supports ranks genes by differential connectivity. The
difference of two biased estimators is not a debiased estimator of
$\Delta_{j\ell}=\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}-\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{\ell}$.

**Estimate $\Delta_{j\ell}$ directly.** D-trace methods target the
difference of precisions without necessarily reconstructing both graphs
first. Zhang and Zou [@zhangSparsePrecisionMatrix2014] introduced the
lasso-penalised D-trace loss for a single sparse precision; the
differential-network extension
[@yuanDifferentialNetworkAnalysis2017] estimates
$\Delta_{j\ell}$. Empirically, D-trace is competitive when the
**difference** is sparser than either graph
[@plaksienkoMethodsDifferentialNetwork2025]. It still does **not**
produce a pair of SPD precisions. A workable **proposal** is: use
D-trace to nominate rewiring genes, then estimate each
$\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{j}$ on that panel with a method from @sec-grn-top4.

`INDEED` multiplies a DE $p$-value by a permutation-filtered change in
partial correlation [@zuoINDEEDIntegratedDifferential2016]. On this
reference the DE $p$-value assumes biological replication
(@nte-pseudoreplication), and the permutation null among cells of one
gastruloid is a technical null. Use it, if at all, as a ranking
heuristic with $p_{g}^{\mathrm{DE}}$ replaced by a fold-change or
between-type score.

### Markov boundaries

Once a GGM exists, seeds (markers, high signal-to-noise genes, D-trace
hits) can be grown by undirected neighbours
$\{g':\omega_{gg'}\neq 0\}$. On a minimal undirected I-map that neighbour
set is the **Markov boundary**, the smallest Markov blanket
[@pearlProbabilisticReasoningIntelligent1988;
@kollerProbabilisticGraphicalModels2009]. That is undirected
separation, not DAG $d$-separation (@sec-separation,
@fig-separation).
